newsitem.title: USA: New car airbag rules to acknowledge their dangers.
newsitem.headline: New car airbag rules to acknowledge their dangers.

text.p: New federal car airbag regulations to be proposed soon will acknowledge that airbags are not the magic safety device once thought and in fact the fast-inflating bags can be fatal to children and small adults.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration is weighing rules that include reducing the high speed of bag inflation, mandating bags with dual speeds for slow and high-speed crashes and letting owners deactivate bags.

Asked if the bloom had worn off airbags, Brian O'Neill, president of the industry-backed Insurance Institute for Highway Safety, said: "Right now it has." He added, "They are wonderful devices, but with tragic side-effects, most of which involve unbelted people."

While they are credited with saving more than 1,100 lives in the past 10 years, airbags are also held responsible for killing at least 30 children -- many of them in front seats or unbuckled -- and 20 small-statured adults.

Bags, which deploy at speeds up to 200 miles an hour, can snap the neck of a child, a small adult or a frail older person. But all involved agree that the danger to children can be averted if they ride buckled up in the rear seat.

When they were introduced, airbags were hailed by safety advocates, car manufacturers and federal highway officials as a highly effective way to prevent deaths in head-on crashes. Initially they were mandated by the NHTSA for the driver side and then gradually phased in for the passenger side too.

But people are now having second thoughts. Manufacturers do not want airbags scrapped but inflated with less power to lessen the risk. The industry, which touted airbags once they were required to install them, petitioned the NHTSA to allow them to depower bags to reduce risks to children and smaller people while continuing to protect larger adults.

Said Andrew Card, president of the American Automobile Manufacturers Association: "The airbag is a highly effective safety device intended to save people." The association said deployment standards were set when few people used seat belts, and now with wider seat belt use the speed can be reduced and passengers still protected.
"Depowering offers the best near-term solution to mitigate airbag risks for all vehicle occupants," it said.

O'Neill's traffic safety group also backs reduced velocity for inflation, saying "there should be an immediate change to allow depowering." People concerned about safety, he said, should be allowed to have dealers reduce the deployment speed.

The advocary group Public Citizen has petitioned the NHTSA to require dual-inflation airbags, which would inflate rapidly in high-speed crashes but slower in less severe crashes. Its president, Joan Claybrook, said this could be done within three years, with depowering a solution only until then.

"The dual inflation bags offer the best solution in the near future as they neither surrender protection for adults in high-speed crashes nor sacrifice low-speed crash protection for children," Public Citizen said.
Another proposal being weighed is to allow car owners to "deactivate" airbags -- something the law, viewing airbags a key safety device, now forbids them to do.
Julie DeFalco, an airbag specialist at the Competitive Enterprise Institute, a conservative research group, backs deactivation. "The best solution is to make them (airbags) optional," she said.

The moves being considered by the NHTSA are considered interim until the industry can develop "smart" airbags that can "sense" when a child or smaller adult is in the passenger seat and reduce the airbag's inflation rate accordingly.
